design_detail: Mendelian randomization within one prospective cohort, the China Kadoorie Biobank (512 715 adults from ten areas of China, recruited 2004-2008 and followed about 10 years to 1 January 2017), set beside conventional analyses of self-reported drinking in the same cohort. 161 498 participants were genotyped for ALDH2 rs671 and ADH1B rs1229984: 151 028 chosen at random (used in all genetic analyses) and 10 470 chosen because they had a stroke or coronary event during follow-up (used only in the disease analyses). In each area, mean male intake was computed for each of the nine joint genotypes, and the 90 area-genotype combinations were grouped into six categories (cut-points 10, 25, 50, 100 and 150 g/week; category means in men 4, 18, 34, 78, 130 and 256 g/week). Disease rates were compared across categories by Cox regression stratified by area and adjusted for age; slopes per 280 g/week were fitted within each area and combined by inverse-variance weighting. Women, few of whom drink, were placed in the same categories to test for effects of the genotypes not mediated by drinking. Labelled prospective-cohort and appraised with ROBINS-E under the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization in one cohort, because the protocol names no instrument for this design.
can_establish: Whether men whose genotype and area predict higher mean alcohol intake, from about 4 to about 256 g/week, have higher or lower rates of stroke and myocardial infarction, in a comparison largely free of the confounding and reverse causation that affect comparisons by self-reported drinking; and whether the U-shape seen with self-reported drinking in the same cohort reappears when people are grouped by genotype instead.
cannot_establish: Effects in women (few drink, so the design uses them only as a check for pleiotropy); effects of beverages other than spirits or of drinking patterns; whether alcohol has a modest effect on myocardial infarction in either direction (1696 genotyped cases; RR 0.96, 0.78 to 1.18 per 280 g/week); the risk at a particular individual intake (categories are group means, and the slopes assume a log-linear relation); and whether part of the genetic effect works through acetaldehyde exposure per drink or faster alcohol clearance rather than through the amount drunk.

sample.recruitment: Community: all permanent residents aged 35-74 without major disability in ten rural and urban areas were to be invited; 499 500 (28% of 1 801 167 invitees) took part, plus 13 215 people just outside the target age range (Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Participants who had already had coronary heart disease, a stroke or a transient ischaemic attack were left out of the incidence analyses (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph). Genetic analyses used the genotyped participants described above.
sample.demographics: Mean age 52 (SD 11); 226 182 urban and 286 533 rural residents; 41% men (editors' calculation, 210 205/512 715). Drinking was mainly of spirits, and the prevalence of weekly drinking varied widely between areas (Results, 1st paragraph; appendix pp 11-12, not read).
sample.attrition: By 1 January 2017, 4781 participants (0.9%) were lost to follow-up and 44 037 (8.6%) had died (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: 28% of invitees took part. The genotyped set adds 10 470 people selected because they had an event, used only in disease analyses; how they were handled in the Cox models is described in the appendix (pp 5-6, not read). Physiological factors other than blood pressure (HDL cholesterol, γ-glutamyltransferase and others) were measured in 18 256 participants of nested case-control studies, not in a random sample.

exposure.measurement: Conventional: self-reported drinking at baseline (main beverage, amount, frequency), classified as current drinkers (drinking in most weeks of the past year), non-drinkers (no drinking in the past year and never a weekly drinker), occasional drinkers (some drinking in the past year but never weekly) and ex-drinkers (formerly weekly drinkers who now drink occasionally or not at all); usual intake estimated from two resurveys of 4-5% of participants to correct for regression dilution (Methods › Alcohol drinking patterns). Genetic: rs671 and rs1229984 genotyped on custom arrays, with genotype frequencies in every area consistent with Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium; assignment to a category depended only on genotype and area, not on a person's own drinking (Methods › Mean alcohol intake by genotype and area).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Units: grams of ethanol per week; the authors equate 100 g/week with one to two drinks per day and 280 g/week with about four drinks per day. Baseline groups of current drinkers: men <140, 140-279, 280-419 and ≥420 g/week; women <70 and ≥70 g/week. Mean usual intake was about 280 g/week in male current drinkers and about 100 g/week in all men (appendix p 12, not read). Genotype effects in men: rs671 AA, AG and GG mean 3, 37 and 157 g/week (1%, 16% and 45% current drinkers); rs1229984 AA, AG and GG 98, 106 and 157 g/week (32%, 33% and 43%). Across the six categories, men's prevalence of ever drinking in most weeks rose from 3% to 74% and mean intake from 4 to 256 g/week; in women intake was below 2 g/week in categories 1-3 and 4 to 8 g/week in categories 4-6 (Figure 2). Occasional drinkers were assigned 5 g/week and ex-drinkers were left out of the category means. No F statistic is reported; mean intake differed more than 50-fold between category 6 and category 1.
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking: the conventional analyses were adjusted for smoking and, in a sensitivity analysis, excluded ever-smokers; the genetic analyses were adjusted only for age (stratified by area), with education, income and smoking added in sensitivity analyses (appendix p 25, not read), and the six categories did not differ much in smoking or other self-reported characteristics (appendix p 19, not read). A published letter (Chen et al., 2019) quotes this paper's data as 61% of men and 71% of current drinkers smoking. Other drugs: not reported.

comparison.controls: Conventional analyses: current drinkers with the lowest intake (men <140 g/week) are the reference (RR=1); non-drinkers, occasional drinkers and ex-drinkers are plotted separately, and their RRs are not printed as numbers (Figures 4 and 5). Genetic analyses: category 1 (mean 4 g/week in men; two-thirds non-drinkers and most of the rest occasional drinkers) is the reference.
comparison.matching: Genetic comparisons are within area (stratified by area) and age-adjusted; conventional comparisons are adjusted for age, area, education, income and smoking.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Genetic analysis: genotype is assigned at conception; A-allele frequencies differ between areas (more common in the south), which the within-area analysis removes. Conventional analysis: reasons for not drinking (illness, former heavy drinking) and lifestyle are only partly captured; sensitivity analyses excluding early follow-up, ever-smokers and people in poor self-reported health left the U-shape in place (appendix pp 23-24, 32, not read).

outcomes.instruments: Linkage by national identification number to hospital records of the national health insurance system (more than 98% coverage in the study areas), local stroke and coronary heart disease registries and death registries; cardiovascular events reviewed and coded to ICD-10. Outcomes: ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, total stroke, acute myocardial infarction and total coronary heart disease (first fatal or non-fatal record of each). Physiological factors: systolic blood pressure at baseline; HDL and LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, lipoprotein(a), C-reactive protein, fibrinogen and γ-glutamyltransferase in the biochemistry subsample.
outcomes.validity_norms: Details of event review are in the appendix (p 4, not read).
outcomes.operationalization: Relative risk (Cox) of each category against the reference; slope expressed as RR per 280 g/week of usual intake (conventional) or of genotype-predicted mean male intake (genetic); adjusted means of physiological factors by category.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the five diseases and eight physiological factors (13); the authors mention allowance for multiple testing only for the further physiological factors examined in women (appendix p 21, not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; record-based coding is unlikely to depend on genotype.

analysis.effect_sizes: [Conventional; men; current drinkers; RR per 280 g/week usual intake; reference lowest-intake current drinkers] ischaemic stroke 1.28 (95% CI 1.19 to 1.38), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.59 (1.37 to 1.85), total stroke 1.35 (1.27 to 1.44), acute myocardial infarction 1.15 (0.96 to 1.38; p=0.14), total coronary heart disease 1.12 (1.04 to 1.21; p=0.003); systolic blood pressure +4.8 mm Hg (4.5 to 5.1). Lower stroke and coronary risks at about 100 g/week than in non-drinkers and ex-drinkers (U-shape), shown in plots only. [Genetic; men; per 280 g/week genotype-predicted mean intake; reference category 1] ischaemic stroke 1.27 (1.13 to 1.43; p=0.0001; 5709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.58 (1.36 to 1.84; 2790 cases), total stroke 1.38 (1.26 to 1.51; 9189 cases); per 100 g/week 1.09 (1.04 to 1.14), 1.18 (1.12 to 1.24) and 1.12 (1.09 to 1.16); acute myocardial infarction 0.96 (0.78 to 1.18; p=0.69; 1696 cases), total coronary heart disease 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17; p=0.40; 6145 cases); systolic blood pressure +4.3 mm Hg (3.7 to 4.9), HDL cholesterol +0.16 mmol/L (0.13 to 0.19), γ-glutamyltransferase +44 IU/L (36 to 53). [Genetic; women; same categories; per 280 g/week of male intake] systolic blood pressure −0.6 mm Hg (−1.0 to −0.1), ischaemic stroke 0.98 (0.88 to 1.09), intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96 (0.82 to 1.12), acute myocardial infarction 0.94 (0.74 to 1.20). [Single variants; men; GG v AG] rs671: stroke 1.19 (1.13 to 1.24), myocardial infarction 1.02 (0.92 to 1.13); rs1229984: stroke 1.19 (1.11 to 1.27), myocardial infarction 1.11 (0.95 to 1.31).
analysis.covariates: Conventional: area, age, education, income and smoking. Genetic: stratified by area and adjusted for age; sensitivity analyses adding education, income and smoking did not change the results materially (appendix p 25, not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or published analysis plan is reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: All five disease outcomes are reported for both approaches. The conventional RRs for non-drinkers and ex-drinkers, on which the U-shape rests, appear only in plots. The category cut-points (10, 25, 50, 100 and 150 g/week) are not justified in the main text; a check pooling the three lowest categories is in the appendix (p 26, not read).
analysis.power: Not reported. The authors call the number of myocardial infarction cases limited, so that some real benefit or hazard cannot be excluded (Discussion, 10th paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In men, self-reported drinking showed the familiar U-shape, with lower stroke and coronary risks at about 100 g/week than in non-drinkers and ex-drinkers. Grouped by genotype and area instead, risk of ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage rose steadily across 4 to 256 g/week of predicted mean intake, with no dip at moderate intake; systolic blood pressure rose by about the same amount per gram in both approaches; and myocardial infarction showed no association (RR 0.96, 0.78 to 1.18). The same genotypes showed no adverse associations in women.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Interpretation states that alcohol "uniformly increases blood pressure and stroke risk" and that its apparent protection against stroke is largely non-causal; Research in context calls the apparently protective associations with stroke largely artifacts of reverse causation and confounding. The genetic results support the absence of a protective dip for stroke, but (1) uniformity rests on a log-linear fit through six category means, and the lowest categories (means 4, 18 and 34 g/week) are estimated imprecisely; (2) the paper does not separate reverse causation from confounding as the cause of the conventional U-shape; (3) the attributable fractions (about 8% of ischaemic strokes and 16% of intracerebral haemorrhages in men) hold, as the authors say, only if there is no protective effect and the relation is log-linear; (4) the excess stroke risk is about twice that expected from the blood-pressure effect, and the explanations offered are untested. For myocardial infarction the Interpretation is appropriately limited (little net effect, in this one study).

timeline.event: Holmes et al. (European ancestry, ADH1B rs1229984 only): carriers of the intake-lowering allele had lower odds of coronary heart disease (OR 0.90) and, in a subset, of ischaemic stroke (0.83), with no association with all stroke. This paper reports its own rs1229984 coronary result as consistent with that study, and its rs671 result as not supporting earlier east Asian meta-analyses (Discussion, 10th paragraph).
This study, published with an accompanying Comment by Yeung and Lam, "Unite for a framework convention for alcohol control" (Lancet 2019;393:1778-1779; doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)32214-1; not read).

Letter by Chen, Ferreira, Mochly-Rosen and Gross (Lancet 2019;394:1617-1618; doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(19)31880-X; read on PMC, PMC7259464): does not dispute the estimates; argues that guidance should take account of the ALDH2 rs671 variant and of the extra acetaldehyde load when smoking and drinking are combined, and asks whether cerebrovascular risk is higher in people who both smoke and drink. Two of its authors declare patents on ALDH2 activation licensed to Foresee Pharmaceuticals.

Mukamal, Stampfer and Rimm, critique of Mendelian randomization evidence on alcohol and cardiovascular disease (Eur J Epidemiol), listed in the project's DOI list as answering the Mendelian randomization studies; not read, and whether it addresses this paper was not checked.

Larsson et al. (European two-sample Mendelian randomization, up to 94 variants): genetically predicted drinking associated with stroke (OR 1.27 per SD of log drinks/week) and more strongly with intracerebral haemorrhage (3.53); Larsson and colleagues describe this as confirming the present stroke findings in European ancestry.

Biddinger et al. (UK Biobank): linear Mendelian randomization associations with stroke (OR 1.26, 1.04 to 1.54; not significant at that paper's corrected threshold) and with coronary artery disease (1.38, 1.10 to 1.74), the latter unlike this study's null myocardial infarction result.

replication.where_it_stands: For stroke, this is the strongest genetic evidence against a protective effect of moderate drinking compared with near-abstention, and European-ancestry Mendelian randomization points the same way, more strongly for intracerebral haemorrhage (Larsson et al., 2020). For myocardial infarction and coronary disease the genetic evidence is inconsistent: null here, positive in European-ancestry studies using ADH1B or many variants (Holmes et al., 2014; Larsson et al., 2020; Biddinger et al., 2022). Two authors (M V Holmes, G Davey Smith) are shared with Holmes et al. (2014), so the two studies are not fully independent.

The funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Role of the funding source; Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Seven authors (IYM, RGW, XWM, SP, RCl, RP, ZC) report grants from the Kadoorie Charitable Foundation, Wellcome Trust, Medical Research Council, GlaxoSmithKline, British Heart Foundation and Cancer Research UK during the study. R Collins reports support from the Nuffield Department of Population Health; grants and personal fees from the British Heart Foundation; grants from Cancer Research UK, the Medical Research Council, Wellcome Trust, Merck & Co, the National Institute for Health Research and Medco; personal fees from UK Biobank; a Pfizer prize for independent research awarded to his department; and a patent for a statin-related myopathy genetic test licensed to the University of Oxford from Boston Heart Diagnostics, with personal benefits waived. All other authors declare no competing interests (Declaration of interests). No ties to the alcohol industry are declared.
funding.affiliations_note: GlaxoSmithKline part-funded the genotyping. M V Holmes, first author of Holmes et al. (2014), and G Davey Smith, an author of that study, are coauthors. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Many more incident myocardial infarctions in genotyped east Asian cohorts (longer follow-up of this cohort, or pooling with other east Asian biobanks), analysed with the same within-area genotype design, to narrow the interval around the null coronary estimate; together with calibration of genotype-predicted intake against repeated objective measures of drinking, to fix the scale of the slopes.

domains.note: Instrument independence: genotype is assigned at conception, and comparisons within area remove differences in allele frequency and drinking culture between areas; little genotype-related difference in smoking or other baseline characteristics (appendix, not read). Exclusion restriction: tested with women as a negative control, in whom the same genotypes predict almost no drinking; women showed no adverse associations with stroke, myocardial infarction, HDL cholesterol or γ-glutamyltransferase, but slightly lower blood pressure (−0.6 mm Hg) and small differences in height, waist and hip, so some path outside drinking exists, and the authors note that the two enzymes act in many pathways. A further route not through the amount drunk: rs671 raises acetaldehyde exposure per drink and rs1229984 speeds alcohol clearance. Pleiotropy-robust multi-variant methods are not applicable to two variants grouped in this way.

Relevance: very strong (category means from 4 to 256 g/week; weekly drinking in men from 3% to 74%), although no F statistic is given. The exposure scale is the self-reported mean intake of men in each category, so under-reporting would make the slopes too steep (the authors say so), and assigning ex-drinkers zero rather than leaving them out would strengthen the slopes by about 10%. Shape at low intake: six categories give a coarse picture below 50 g/week; no excess risk was seen in category 1, where two-thirds do not drink, but the lowest categories are imprecise.

Selection into the cohort: 28% of invitees, aged 35-74, with people with prior vascular disease excluded; for a genetic comparison this matters only if taking part depended on both genotype-driven drinking and vascular risk. The disease analyses add 10 470 people genotyped because they had an event, and their handling in the Cox models is described only in the appendix (not read).
Not applicable in the usual sense: genotype is fixed, and changes in drinking over life are part of the genetic contrast.
0.9% lost to follow-up; the genotyped subset was chosen at random apart from the added cases.
Record linkage to insurance hospital data with more than 98% coverage, disease registries and death registries, coded to ICD-10; unlikely to depend on genotype.

No registered plan; the category cut-points were chosen by the authors without justification in the main text, and the conventional non-drinker and ex-drinker RRs are not given as numbers; all five diseases are reported for both approaches.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The genetic stroke result is among the best-protected estimates of an effect of alcohol available: strong instruments, comparisons within area, a sex in which the genotypes barely change drinking as a negative control, near-complete follow-up by record linkage, and many events. Concerns remain about effects of the genotypes that do not run through the amount drunk (acetaldehyde per drink, small differences in women) and about the coarse resolution at the lowest intakes. The conventional analyses in the same paper are at high risk of confounding and reverse causation, as the authors themselves argue, and serve here only to show the U-shape that the genetic analysis does not reproduce. Design label and instrument follow the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization (the protocol is silent). Cite this card for: genotype-predicted alcohol intake in Chinese men associated log-linearly with higher risk of ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage across 4 to 256 g/week, with no sign of a protective dip at moderate intake; similar blood-pressure effects in genetic and conventional analyses. Do not cite it for: effects in women, a precise null for myocardial infarction, wine or drinking patterns, or the attributable fractions without their stated conditions.

key_findings.finding: 512 715 adults from ten areas of China were enrolled in 2004-2008 (28% of invitees aged 35-74, plus 13 215 just outside that range; mean age 52, SD 11) and followed for about 10 years to 1 January 2017; 4781 (0.9%) were lost to follow-up and 44 037 (8.6%) died.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 33% of men (69 897/210 205) and 2% of women (6245/302 510) drank in most weeks, mostly spirits, and the proportion varied widely between areas.

Genotype and intake in men: rs671 AA, AG and GG mean 3, 37 and 157 g/week, with 1%, 16% and 45% current drinkers; rs1229984 AA, AG and GG 98, 106 and 157 g/week, with 32%, 33% and 43%. A-allele frequencies 0.21 for rs671 (0.13-0.29 by area) and 0.69 for rs1229984 (0.64-0.74). Within single areas, mean male intake ran from 2 to 443 g/week across genotypes in Sichuan and from 1 to 29 g/week in Gansu.

The six genotype-area categories had mean male intakes of 4, 18, 34, 78, 130 and 256 g/week, and the proportion of men who had ever drunk in most weeks was 3%, 15%, 20%, 39%, 60% and 74%; in women the proportions were below 1% in categories 1-3 and 2%, 5% and 6% in categories 4-6, with mean intake below 2 g/week in categories 1-3 and 4, 5 and 8 g/week in categories 4-6.
key_findings.note: Category values are printed on the bars of Figure 2 (an image), read from the full-size figure image.

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure in men: systolic blood pressure rose by 4.8 mm Hg (95% CI 4.5 to 5.1) per 280 g/week of usual intake among current drinkers (conventional; 193 003 men) and by 4.3 mm Hg (3.7 to 4.9) per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean intake (genetic; 55 897 men in Figure 3). HDL cholesterol rose by 0.19 (0.17 to 0.22) and 0.16 (0.13 to 0.19) mmol/L, and γ-glutamyltransferase by 62 (54 to 70) and 44 (36 to 53) IU/L, in the conventional and genetic analyses respectively.
key_findings.note: The HDL and γ-glutamyltransferase slopes and the sample sizes are printed in Figure 3 (an image), read from the full-size figure image.

key_findings.finding: Conventional stroke analysis in men: U-shaped associations of self-reported intake with ischaemic stroke (14 930 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage (3496) and total stroke (19 859), with lower risk at about 100 g/week than in non-drinkers and, even more, ex-drinkers. In current drinkers, RR per 280 g/week usual intake 1.28 (1.19 to 1.38) for ischaemic stroke and 1.59 (1.37 to 1.85) for intracerebral haemorrhage (difference p=0.01); total stroke 1.35 (1.27 to 1.44). The U-shape remained when the first years of follow-up, ever-smokers or people reporting poor health were excluded. Reference: current drinkers with the lowest intake.
key_findings.note: Case numbers and the total-stroke slope are printed in Figure 4 (an image); the RRs of non-drinkers, occasional drinkers and ex-drinkers are plotted without numbers and were not extracted.

key_findings.finding: Genetic stroke analysis in men: no U-shape; risk rose steadily across genotype-predicted mean intake of 4-256 g/week; RR per 280 g/week 1.27 (1.13 to 1.43; p=0.0001) for ischaemic stroke (5709 cases), 1.58 (1.36 to 1.84; p<0.0001) for intracerebral haemorrhage (2790 cases; difference p=0.01) and 1.38 (1.26 to 1.51) for total stroke (9189 cases); per 100 g/week 1.09 (1.04 to 1.14), 1.18 (1.12 to 1.24) and 1.12 (1.09 to 1.16). Adjusting for potential confounders did not change the results materially.

There was no sign of increased stroke risk at the lowest genotype-predicted intake (category 1, in which two-thirds were non-drinkers) and no material departure from a log-linear relation; pooling categories 1-3 (about 25 g/week) against categories 4-5 (about 100 g/week) still showed adverse rather than protective associations for ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage, and findings in each area were directionally consistent.

Conventional coronary analysis in men: U-shaped associations, with substantially lower rates of acute myocardial infarction (2958 cases) and total coronary heart disease (14 326) at moderate intake than in non-drinkers or ex-drinkers; among current drinkers RR per 280 g/week 1.15 (0.96 to 1.38; p=0.14) for myocardial infarction and 1.12 (1.04 to 1.21; p=0.003) for total coronary heart disease. Reference: current drinkers with the lowest intake.

Genetic coronary analysis in men: no clear association; RR per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean intake 0.96 (0.78 to 1.18; p=0.69) for acute myocardial infarction (1696 cases) and 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17; p=0.40) for total coronary heart disease (6145 cases).

Women as a check for pleiotropy (same six categories; effects per 280 g/week of mean male intake): systolic blood pressure −0.6 mm Hg (−1.0 to −0.1; men +4.3); HDL cholesterol 0.00 (−0.03 to 0.03); γ-glutamyltransferase 0 (−3 to 3) IU/L; ischaemic stroke RR 0.98 (0.88 to 1.09; men 1.27); intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96 (0.82 to 1.12; men 1.58); acute myocardial infarction 0.94 (0.74 to 1.20; men 0.96). P for a larger effect in men than in women <0.0001 for blood pressure, HDL, γ-glutamyltransferase and intracerebral haemorrhage, 0.0007 for ischaemic stroke and 0.45 for myocardial infarction. After allowing for multiple testing, women showed small genotype-related increases in height, waist and hip only.

Single-variant analyses in men (one copy of the variant allele; GG v AG): rs671 stroke RR 1.19 (1.13 to 1.24), myocardial infarction 1.02 (0.92 to 1.13); rs1229984 stroke 1.19 (1.11 to 1.27), myocardial infarction 1.11 (0.95 to 1.31). In women, neither variant was significantly associated with stroke or heart disease.

If, and only if, there is no protective effect and the relation is log-linear, the genetic estimates imply that alcohol caused about 8% of ischaemic strokes and 16% of intracerebral haemorrhages among the men; the excess stroke risks are about twice what the blood-pressure effect alone would predict.

The authors state that if intake was under-reported, all their dose-response slopes are too steep, and that counting ex-drinkers as zero intake instead of leaving them out would have made the genetic slopes about 10% stronger; effects of drinks other than spirits could not be assessed.

reporting_issues.issue: The genetic systolic blood pressure analysis in men is given as n=55 879 in the heading of Table 2 and as n=55 897 in Figure 3D.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor transposition; either figure can be quoted only with the location stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The conventional U-shape is stated in words and plotted, but the RRs of non-drinkers, occasional drinkers and ex-drinkers against the reference group are not given as numbers anywhere in the main text.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 7th and 10th paragraphs; Figures 4 and 5
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the apparent protective association in the conventional analysis cannot be quoted from this paper's text; claims should describe it qualitatively or take the values from the appendix after it is read.

reporting_issues.issue: The phrase that genotype-predicted mean male intake ranged from 4 to 256 g/week (Summary) refers to category means; individual genotype-area combinations ranged up to 443 g/week (Results, 4th paragraph).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Summary › Findings; Results, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Not an error, but claims should say that the range refers to group means.
